newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile's Aninat sees 96 inflation at 6.6 pct tops.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Aninat sees 96 inflation at 6.6 pct tops.

text.p: Chilean inflation for the year will stand at no more than a tenth of a percentage point above the official target of 6.5 percent, and may be slightly less, Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat said.
A key adviser to Aninat also said Chile's trade deficit would end the year at about $1 billion, higher than most projections, and would end 1997 at about the same level.

''On inflation, in the worst of all cases, we'll be about one-tenth of a point higher than the target, at 6.6 percent. In the best case, we'll end the year at 6.4 percent,'' Aninat told foreign reporters.

The 1996 result, after 8.2 percent last year and a projected 5.5 percent in 1997, will mark progress in Chile's long-term campaign to bring its inflation down to levels like those in developed countries by the end of the decade, he said.
''It becomes more and more difficult to bring inflation down,'' he said.

''Inflation at three or four percent is perfectly viable and possible for Chile. Less than three percent? I'm not going to slit my wrists or go crazy trying to get inflation below that level because I think be like seeking a precious gem,'' he said.

The ministry's coordinator of economic policy, Jose de Gregorio, said the trade deficit could end this year at about $1 billion and at a more or less similar level in 1997 because no major change in prices for Chilean exports is expected.
The 1996 deficit, though wider than recent estimates of around $800 million to $850 million, is completely manageable as a percentage of Chile's gross domestic product, he said.
''It's an absolutely sustainable figure for a developing country like Chile,'' said de Gregorio.

He attributed the deficit to unfavorable terms of trade for Chilean exports. Aninat added that the peso's strength against the dollar has also encouraged manufacturers to import more capital goods and modernize, accounting for part of the gap.
''In the past six years, this country has imported more capital goods than in decades,'' he said.
''Businessmen say, while the exchange rate is low, let's make the most of it by renovating all our machinery,'' he said.
Chile's most pressing economic problem continued to be its uneven distribution of income, which is slightly better than the Latin American average but still much too skewed against the poor, he said.
''We're better in that field than Brazil, for example, but much worse than Costa Rica or Uruguay,'' he said.

''The problem isn't that anyone's getting poorer. No one is falling. The problem is that (income for) the poor grows five percent and the rich grows 10 percent,'' thus further widening the gap between them, said Aninat.
